function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a practical guide you can follow (or copy‑paste into your terminal) to get everything set up in the **nodejs-welcome** repository.  
I’ll walk through each step, show you the exact commands you’d run, and provide the file contents you’ll need to create or update.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH access set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you prefer HTTPS, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` and authenticate with your credentials.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & Create Required Files

### 2.1 Inspect the Repo

Run a quick check to see what’s already there:

```bash
# List top‑level files
ls -la

# Show the existing Dockerfile (if any)
cat Dockerfile || echo "No Dockerfile found"

# Show the existing Kubernetes manifests (if any)
find . -name '*.yaml' -o -name '*.yml'
```

> **What to look for:**  
> * Does a `Dockerfile` exist?  
> * Are there any `.yaml` or `.yml` files under a `k8s/` or `deploy/` folder?  
> * Is there a `package.json` that lists dependencies?  

If you find an existing Dockerfile or Kubernetes files, you can either overwrite them or keep them as backups (`mv Dockerfile Dockerfile.bak`, etc.).

---

### 2.2 Create/Update the Dockerfile

Create a new `Dockerfile` (or overwrite the existing one) with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node.js runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
EXPOSE 3000

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Run the application
CMD [ "npm", "start" ]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and includes only the essentials.  
> * `npm ci` ensures reproducible installs from `package-lock.json`.  
> * `CMD ["npm", "start"]` assumes your `package.json` has a `"start"` script that runs the server (common for Express apps).

---

### 2.3 Create Kubernetes Deployment & Service

Create a directory for Kubernetes manifests (if it doesn’t exist):

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
cd k8s
```

#### Deployment (`deployment.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
```

#### Service (`service.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # Change to NodePort or ClusterIP if you don’t want external LB
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **How to apply locally (optional):**

```bash
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f service.yaml
```

---

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a directory for GitHub Actions workflows:

```bash
mkdir -p .github/workflows
```

Create a file named `ci.yml` inside that directory with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    - name: Cache npm dependencies
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: ~/.npm
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-node-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-node-

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
        docker tag zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Push Docker image
      run: |
        docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Important:**  
> * Add two secrets to your GitHub repo settings:  
>   * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username.  
>   * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (create one in Docker Hub → Settings → Security).  
> * The workflow builds the image on every push to `main`, tags it with the commit SHA and `latest`, then pushes both tags.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage All Changes

```bash
# From the root of the repo
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you had an old Dockerfile or Kubernetes files, they’re now staged for commit (you can review with `git status`).

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, GitHub Actions will automatically trigger the workflow you just added.  
> You can monitor the build at **Actions → CI** in the GitHub UI.

---

### Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Task |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Cloned repo |
| ✅ | Created/updated `Dockerfile` |
| ✅ | Added `k8s/deployment.yaml` & `k8s/service.yaml` |
| ✅ | Added GitHub Actions workflow (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) |
| ✅ | Staged all new files |
| ✅ | Committed & pushed to `main` |

Once the CI pipeline passes, you’ll have a Docker image built and pushed to Docker Hub, ready to deploy via the Kubernetes manifests you just created. Happy coding!
